items.title: Southern and central Australia face summer of heightened bushfire risk and heatwaves
items.summary:
Fire chiefs say large swathes of the country are at risk from fires driven by high fuel loads, dry soil and hot weather

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Large parts of southern and central Australia face elevated fire risk this summer, authorities say, while heatwaves and extreme temperatures are likely nationwide.

Most of Victoria, eastern Tasmania and large parts of South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales and the Northern Territory face heightened bushfire risk – driven by high fuel loads, low soil moisture and forecast hot and dry conditions – according to the seasonal outlook from the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC), released on Friday.

items.title: ‘Disaster’ unfolding as Sydney fire ant outbreak partly blamed on ignored biosecurity recommendations

Years-old recommendations by Australia’s biosecurity watchdog have been ignored or not acted on by successive federal governments, increasing the risk of an invasive pest outbreak such as the fire ants discovered in Sydney this week, according to experts.

Environmentalists and biosecurity experts warn the large colony of red imported fire ants is a warning sign that the country’s quarantine system is too slow-moving, underfunded and overly concerned with agriculture.

items.title: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds
items.summary:
Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain

Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found.

The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991.

items.t: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds

items.title: Suit alleges Louisiana land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil violates open meetings law
items.summary:
Suit says parish board was manipulated to allow deal to go through and settlement agreement hidden from public

After ending a lawsuit over ExxonMobil’s damage to wetlands, Louisiana officials moved quickly to approve a deal giving SpaceX access to 125,000 acres (50,600 hectares) of marsh formerly owned by the oil company. A new lawsuit now alleges they did so in violation of the state’s open meetings law.

The lawsuit, filed by three south-central Louisiana residents, follows state and Vermilion parish officials’ approval of what is estimated to be a record $27.5bn tax incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project, announced over the summer. The officials violated the state’s open meetings law eight times while facilitating the agreement in attempts to “keep the public in the dark about what they are doing for SpaceX”, the lawsuit alleges.

items.title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
items.summary:
It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical

In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy

Continue reading...
items.t: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures

items.title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses
items.summary:
Beaches close as Los Angeles and La Jolla see all-time high tides and big waves batter landmark pier in Pacifica

Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.

As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported, and collapsed after contact with ocean swells 12 times stronger than on an average November day.

items.t: California beaches close as record-breaking tides and major flooding loom

The US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) food safety and inspection service (FSIS) and some states conduct regular checks for salmonella and other bacteria in commercial poultry plants. Salmonella can live in the intestines of poultry, and it can cause nausea, diarrhea and even death in humans if meat is not cooked properly and then consumed.

The US army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of the the bomb-making material lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

items.title: Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline
items.summary:
Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer said Tuesday that she’s pausing both pending and issued state permits for the plan to replace a segment of the Line 5 oil pipeline beneath the Straits of Mackinac.

Whitmer said regulators at the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or EGLE, need to answer questions about the full scope of the plan’s threats to the environment.

Those questions, according to Whitmer, were raised by a Michigan Supreme Court ruling this summer on a related Line 5 tunnel permit. Justices tossed out a permit issued by a separate state agency, saying their review of environmental harms was too narrow. 

Line 5 has been transporting oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles between Ontario and Wisconsin since 1954. A 4-mile segment passes through the Straits of Mackinac, the narrow waterways that connect Lake Michigan to Lake Huron, separating Michigan’s Lower and Upper peninsulas. Sensitive coastal and wetlands habitats are found in the straits, and the area is sacred to Anishinaabe peoples , featuring prominently in their creation story and serving as burial grounds for their ancestors. 

“I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water,” Whitmer, whose second and final term will end January 1, said in the announcement. “Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life.” The permit pause comes weeks after regulators in Wisconsin had been dealing with a spill on the portion of Line 5 that crosses that state.

It’s the latest setback for pipeline owner Enbridge Energy, which…
items.t: Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline

items.title: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?
items.summary:
The headlines say what people already know: Food is getting more expensive. Consumers have been feeling an uptick in the overall price of both dining out and preparing meals at home this year, according to numbers from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. 

And just in time for the holidays, things seem to be getting worse. The American Farm Bureau Federation found that the price of goods usually found in a Thanksgiving dinner increased this year for the first time since 2022. One economist told Bloomberg that Americans should expect food prices to keep creeping up into next year. 

The high price of fuel, driven by the war in Iran, has contributed to the sticker shock Americans are feeling at the grocery store. Farmers need diesel to harvest, process, store, and transport produce and other crops from the field to retailers. Climate change, as well as El Niño spurring extreme weather globally, is also at play. 

And yet, however flummoxed U.S. consumers may be about the high costs of living — a major driver of the midterms’ “ blue wave ” — consumer spending has only gone up. In fact, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of the U.S. gross domestic product , or GDP, and has driven the economy for some time , increased by 3.8 percent in the third quarter of this year.

At the same time, food systems are still responsible for somewhere between a quarter and a third of global greenhouse gas emissions . With food prices creeping up, it’s worth asking whatever happened to the idea of consumers as climate or environmental activists. The concept of “voting with your…
items.t: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?

items.title: The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry
items.summary:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and KERA, a public media organization serving the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex. 

This month’s midterm elections featured a previously unthinkable result in Texas: Democrats won every single statewide race in the Lone Star State. Some of those newly elected Democrats have become household names, like Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. But the list of Democratic victors also includes a centrist set to occupy a little-known office with outsize influence over the country’s oil and gas industry. 

Jon Rosenthal won a contentious race for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission against Republican Bo French, whose racist social media posts drew national bipartisan backlash . Rosenthal, the first Democrat elected to the commission since 1990, isn’t trying to usher in radical change, and his influence will be limited by the two Republicans already sitting on the commission. But he’s aiming to bring transparency, accountability, and a bigger budget to the regulatory board.

“Voters have delivered a mandate for a change,” said Rosenthal at a post-election press conference . “My top priority … is doubling the Railroad Commission’s budget. I believe the commission needs more resources to do the work they are [tasked] to do.”

The Railroad Commission was established in 1891 to regulate the rail industry. Over the years, the agency’s focus shifted to overseeing the state’s booming oil and gas industry. In 2024, Texas accounted for almost half of the country’s crude oil production. This fact…
items.t: The ‘drill baby drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry

items.title: What to know about the Army’s lead detonation in Iowa
items.summary:
After months of planning, days of warnings, and the fear of a plume of lead dust, the destruction of nearly 5 tons of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa was over in seconds.

For all the concern about what might happen when the U.S. Army blew up 68 drums of lead azide on Wednesday, the detonation itself proved remarkably uneventful. Two booms sounded across a clear, cold winter morning just after 9 a.m., each creating a wispy white plume that quickly dissipated. State and federal officials said the operation appeared to have gone as planned, and more than an hour later, the Environmental Protection Agency’s real-time air monitors had detected no airborne lead .

Officials had warned that the detonation could send lead-laden dust over homes and farmland for miles around. The EPA deployed 300 employees and contractors and collected more than 1,200 air, soil, dust, and water samples before the blast to establish a baseline. Early air-monitoring results suggest the elaborate precautions the Army took may have limited the amount of airborne lead. Post-blast sampling is now underway to determine where lead was deposited and whether cleanup is necessary.

The operation followed days of controversy, evacuations, and shelter-in-place warnings, as well as objections from elected officials in Iowa and Illinois and an unsuccessful legal effort by environmental groups to stop it. Here’s what to know about why the Army undertook the unusual operation, the risks it posed, and what officials are watching for now.

items.title: A walkable city of tomorrow is growing in suburban Utah
items.summary:
Sarah Miller biked with her 5-year-old son on a hot afternoon this summer to a vibrant new park in Utah City, a community rising on 700 acres in the heart of Vineyard, one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, and envisioned as its new downtown.

They rode along the Greenline, a wide promenade flanked by pickleball, tennis, and basketball courts that runs through the development, from the FrontRunner train station toward glittering Utah Lake. Miller said she moved with her kids a few ago to live by the lakeshore, and she’s enjoyed watching Utah City go up near her home.

Its first two swanky apartment complexes, called simply 120 and 220 Bend, were finished in February, though only a few balconies had patio furniture. Miller and her son had the park, with its array of slides and wooden play structures to explore, almost to themselves.

“It’s very quiet for now,” Miller said. “I imagine as it grows, more people will come in, and it will feel a bit more alive, but I think it’s beautiful.”

Utah City’s developer is building on a rare opportunity to create a transit-oriented, high-density community from scratch in the middle of one of the country’s fastest-growing metro areas — with strong support from former Vineyard city officials, new tools from the local government to help with financing, and investments from taxpayers. It currently has 1,400 units for rent. 

The new community has spread across property that was once home to Geneva Steel, an industrial complex built during World War II that went defunct in the 2000s. Former Vineyard officials created tax incentives to clean…
items.t: A walkable city of tomorrow is growing in suburban Utah

items.title: Voters are fed up with for-profit utilities, but they keep rejecting ‘public power’
items.summary:
Climate activists around the country saw this month’s midterm elections as a win. From congressional seats to governors’ mansions to local offices, progressive candidates leveraged voters’ frustration with the rising cost of living, especially high power bills, to defeat fossil fuel-friendly challengers.

But voters in two communities — Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Kitsap County, Washington — also rejected an idea that some say can address both climate change and affordability: replacing for-profit utilities with publicly owned ones. 

On average, public utilities in the country charge lower electric rates and offer more reliable service than for-profit providers. Advocates contend that by being accountable to communities, they could transition to cleaner forms of energy faster than their counterparts beholden to shareholders and bottom lines.

Despite being in different regions of the country, the two community efforts unfolded in eerily similar ways. In each, private utilities spent roughly $2 million on local opposition campaigns, even using identical terms, like “too costly” and “too risky.” In the end, both initiatives failed, sharing the same fate as the vast majority of recent public power efforts around the country. 

These results highlight the unique challenges of creating a new public power utility in the 21st century. A century ago, building a new public utility meant building a new grid. Today, it means buying out the poles and wires already owned by a for-profit utility, a process that more closely resembles a hostile takeover.

items.t: Voters are fed up with for-profit utilities, but they keep rejecting ‘public power’

items.title: Nepal hoped for flood aid at COP31. It got nothing.
items.summary:
When almost 200 countries endorsed the Paris Agreement in 2015 , they agreed to a massive transfer of money between the world’s largest carbon emitters and the poor countries on the front lines of climate change. The accord promised that developed countries would begin “mobilizing climate finance” in “a progression beyond previous efforts,” with a focus on “public and grant-based resources” as opposed to loans that poor countries would have to pay back. This money would help develop clean energy projects like solar and wind farms, as well as sea walls, water wells, and other projects that could help the Global South adapt to extreme weather. For countries already facing down climate disasters, it would pay to help them recover from the loss and damage caused by these events.

The reality has been a lot uglier. These promises were always voluntary, or at least impossible to enforce, and rich countries have failed to meet most of their obligations. They have provided most clean energy finance through loans, which have strained the budgets of many poor countries. They have failed to cut their own emissions fast enough to slow down global warming, which has increased the cost of adapting to a warmer world. They have failed to provide money for that adaptation, which has increased the scale of loss and damage. And they have failed to provide money for loss and damage, which has forced developing countries to spend their own money on recovery from extreme weather. 

In recent years this financial failure has all but derailed the United Nations climate process, in which countries…
items.t: Nepal hoped for flood aid at COP31. It got nothing.

items.title: How COP31 became climate diplomacy’s ‘darkest moment’
items.summary:
No one expected the 31st Conference of the Parties to be game-changing — from the start, everyone called it an “implementation” COP — but those gathered in Antalya, Turkey, hoped it would at least maintain momentum on clean energy development. They also wanted to see countries reaffirm their commitment to multilateral climate action amid heightened geopolitical tension. 

Instead, the talks collapsed after two weeks of negotiations that ran nearly 50 hours into overtime — longer than ever before. More than 90 nations, including the Marshall Islands, the United Kingdom, and the entire European Union, objected to a draft of the high-level political agreement, called a cover decision, that typically caps each COP because it omitted the words “fossil fuels” and left key details about climate finance unaddressed. 

“We will not endorse an Antalya pact or cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien said during a closing plenary. “The draft put before us does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face, and therefore the EU cannot accept it.”

In an unusual arrangement, this year’s negotiations were run by ministers from Turkey and Australia. It was the first climate conference since COP15 in 2009 to founder over a cover decision, something many nations blamed on shoddy management by the hosts.

This time, the breakdown came at a time of even greater peril. The world is being racked by extreme heat , raging wildfires , and devastating floods , and it is on the brink of…
items.t: How COP31 became climate diplomacy’s ‘darkest moment’

items.title: The world doesn’t need solar or wind — it needs both
items.summary:
Humans are still hunter-gatherers — not for food, but for energy. Much like we once roamed the landscape digging up edible roots, today we gouge the planet for coal, oil, and gas. But just as we eventually adopted agriculture, we’re starting to farm the wind and sun. Because we can’t stop our star from setting, though, we must combine solar panels with large batteries, which load up on energy during the day and distribute it at night. 

According to a new report from the energy think tank Ember, diversifying the electrical grid by adding wind power is a massive opportunity to reduce costs. “If you rely on one crop and that crop is having a bad year, you’re going to be struggling,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember and author of the new report. “The same is true for wind and solar, and it’s the reason why diversification is so important. We’re now building batteries, and those are effectively the silos where we store the sunshine for later in the day.”

The report found that in the United States and Europe, you’d need 20 hours of battery storage to achieve 90 percent uptime for solar. Add wind power to the system and that drops to just 12 hours, meaning you don’t have to install as many costly lithium -ion batteries . Accordingly, worldwide this technique could drop the median cost of meeting that 90 percent demand from $105 per megawatt-hour with solar to $86 with additional wind power. (You can see the potential of that wind power in the map below — it alone can more than meet electricity demand.)

items.title: El Niño is already scrambling your ski season
items.summary:
Being open for Thanksgiving has long been a goal for major ski resorts, including Sugarbush in Vermont. It had planned to have its lifts running and its slopes swarming by now. But with highs approaching 60 degrees Fahrenheit for much of the past week, that hasn’t happened.

”It’s been a really warm November,” said John Bleh, director of communications at Sugarbush. “New snowmaking technology has helped a ton, but it’s not the ultimate cure-all.”

The popular destination is one of a slew throughout the East, from Sugarloaf in Maine to Snowshoe Mountain in West Virginia, that have had to delay opening due to unseasonably balmy conditions.

On the other side of the country, skiers in California are gloating. Resorts in the Lake Tahoe area received more than 4 feet of snow after a recent series of storms. The bounty was so generous that the Sierra Avalanche Center was warning of a “considerable” risk of slides and Kirkwood Mountain Resort opened nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. “It’s always exciting to get the season underway, but being able to open this early is a huge win,” Ricky Newberry, the resort’s general manager, said in a statement .

It’s a bit more complicated in the Rockies. Some resorts in Utah and Colorado got off to a slow start before recent storms brought snow, but Wolf Creek in the southern end of the state has opened all of its terrain . 

These wildly different starts to the ski season are a clear sign that the “super” or “Godzilla” El Niño, the strongest on record, is already shaping what could be a weird winter on the slopes.

items.title: How wildfire litigation became big business in America
items.summary:
On a November morning in 2018, the foothills of the Sierra Nevada were primed to burn. Northern California had received little rainfall, and the grasses and shrubs above the town of Paradise were bone dry. Humidity levels were dangerously low as winds up to 40 miles per hour gusted downslope toward the 26,000-person community.

When a live wire broke free from a 99-year-old transmission tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Paradise stood little chance. 

The arcing wire ignited the brush below to start the Camp Fire, which claimed the lives of 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures in a matter of hours, charring whole neighborhoods to displace tens of thousands of people. It was the deadliest wildfire in California’s history.

But another metric would later come to define the fire that destroyed Paradise.

Thousands of victims sued PG&E. The utility eventually agreed to settle their claims for $13.5 billion in compensation for the Camp Fire, as well as other blazes ignited by its equipment in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. It was one of the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history, driving the company to bankruptcy and demonstrating that utilities could be held liable for huge sums when faulty equipment ignites conflagrations.

items.t: How wildfire litigation became big business in America
